description: EN: Team Janssen, named after the lava exoplanet 55 Cancri e. Flame in Freefall: an AI dashboard that turns NASA microgravity combustion data into evidence-based fire safety insights. Data science, ML, web dev. Rosario, Argentina. ES: Equipo Janssen. Tablero con IA que convierte datos de combustión en microgravedad de NASA en conclusiones de seguridad contra incendios. Ciencia de datos, ML, desarrollo web. Image: ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser (CC BY 4.0).
summary: If a fire starts aboard a spacecraft or a future Moon or Mars habitat, will it go out by itself, and how fast? We built a web dashboard that answers that question from NASA's own microgravity combustion experiments. From NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system we curated 1,870 tests from 24 investigations. On the three experiment families that record how each flame ended (FLEX fuel droplets, ACME CFI-G gas flames and BASS solid materials), we trained interpretable machine-learning models. A researcher picks a fire and an atmosphere (oxygen, pressure, CO₂, helium), moves the "sensor" readings, and immediately sees whether a flame tends to keep burning or to go out, how long it lasts, where the outcome flips, and which real NASA tests back it. An assistant explains the result in plain language using only the models' numbers and passages from NASA reports. Where NASA never tested a combination, the dashboard shows gray ("unknown, not safe") instead of extrapolating. This matters because proposed exploration habitats plan about 34 % oxygen at low pressure, an atmosphere NASA's data barely covers.
details:
What it does

Flame in Freefall turns decades of NASA microgravity fire experiments into answers a researcher, engineer or student can use in seconds. In every NASA test behind our models a flame was lit on purpose; the question we answer is what happens next.

  • "If a flame starts here, does it keep burning?" For a chosen fire (methanol or n-heptane droplet; ethane, propane or butane gas flame) and atmosphere (oxygen, pressure, CO₂, helium), a traffic light and the chance the flame keeps burning, with its 95 % interval.
  • "What changed?" Move a reading as a sensor would and the panel shows before → now. Example: raising oxygen from 21 % to 40 % turns a propane flame from "goes out by itself in ~8 s" into "keeps burning, ~131 s" (NASA's real flames under those conditions: 8 s and 124 s).
  • "Where does it flip?" A curve for the variable being moved marks where the chance of keeping burning crosses 50 %, or says that it flips inside a range NASA never tested.
  • "How long does it last?" For gas flames, a survival curve (share of flames still burning over time) next to the burn times of the closest real NASA tests.
  • "Why?" A chat assistant answers questions in English or Spanish (predictions, ranges and thresholds, rankings, data gaps, explanations of the phenomenon) and shows its sources: models, NASA tests and report passages.
  • "Where did NASA test?" A map of oxygen against pressure shows every tested condition and, above all, the empty ones. Gray always means "unknown, not safe".

How it works

  1. Data. We downloaded the 22 experimental tables of the 24 NASA PSI (Physical Sciences Informatics) combustion investigations, plus logs, reports and papers (315 documents). Each test was loaded into PostgreSQL with its source file and row. How each flame ended was coded from NASA's logs and reports with explicit rules, checked by hand; every data decision is logged with its reason (33 data decisions).
  2. Interpretable models. FLEX droplets (275 tests): regularized logistic regression of "the flame goes out before the droplet is used up", with fuel interactions; grouped cross-validation (tests run together are never split between training and checking): AUC 0.91. ACME CFI-G gas flames (333 tests): Cox survival model of the time until the flame goes out by itself (C-index 0.82 normal flames, 0.71 inverse flames); ignition shown as NASA's observed shares. BASS / BASS-II solids (250 tests): evidence only. Every prediction carries a domain rule: if NASA never tested something close to the asked combination, the answer is "unknown", not a number.
  3. Assistant with guardrails. The language model computes nothing. A planner calls the tools (the models, a whitelisted search over the curated tables, a hybrid vector + full-text search over NASA reports). The system, not the language model, decides whether a question can be answered, partly answered or not answered. The language model only writes the text from that evidence, and a verifier checks every number, citation and substance against it, falling back to a plain template answer when the text does not pass.

Results (measured, not claimed)

  • Blind test with 40 questions the system had never seen, written by agents without access to the project (teachers, students, engineers, the public; English and Spanish; out-of-scope questions included): the question type was recognized in 31/40 and the right decision (answer / partial / abstain) was taken in 37/40.
  • After a night-long self-inspection, invented whole numbers slipping past the verifier dropped from 38–78 % to 0–3 %.
  • Model durations checked against NASA's real flames: they match at 21 % O₂ (ethane, propane) and for propane at 40 % O₂.

Known limitations

  • No partial gravity: NASA PSI has no lunar or Martian gravity combustion data; such questions are flagged.
  • Solids were tested only up to 22.7 % O₂ and at about 1 atm; they are shown as evidence, never predicted.
  • Gas-flame duration at 40 % O₂: for butane and ethane the model's median is 2–4× longer than NASA's observed flames (propane matches), so durations are shown as model estimates next to the real NASA times.
  • Droplets have no duration model (only observed burn times); FLEX "disruption" outcomes are partly caused by a fuel contaminant reported by NASA, so we show a sensitivity range.
  • The assistant still misclassifies about 1 in 5 new questions and sometimes phrases things loosely; it runs on a free-tier language model service with a daily quota, and when the quota is used up the chat answers with plain templates (same numbers, less fluent).
  • It is an indicator built from laboratory experiments, not a certified fire alarm.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Habitat and vehicle designers can compare candidate cabin atmospheres before choosing one, with the evidence and its limits in view.
  • Fire suppression: quantify how inert gases help (e.g. +5 points of CO₂ roughly doubles the odds that a heptane droplet flame goes out, ×1.98).
  • Researchers get the gray zones as a to-do list of missing experiments: solids above 22.7 % O₂, low-pressure oxygen-rich mixes, partial gravity.
  • Students and teachers can explore real NASA data with the uncertainty shown, not hidden. On Earth, oxygen-rich places such as hospitals and hyperbaric chambers face the same question.

What makes it creative

Instead of a chatbot over documents, the "brain" is a set of interpretable models trained on NASA's test outcomes; the language model only explains what those models and the data say. Uncertainty is part of the product: intervals, observed NASA times beside every estimate, and an explicit gray "unknown, not safe" wherever NASA never tested.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty over coverage (no extrapolation outside tested conditions); interpretability (logistic and survival models whose effects can be read and checked); validation that does not leak (grouped cross-validation); auditability (every number traceable to a NASA test, file and row, and every data decision logged); and users without a combustion background (plain-language labels, English and Spanish).

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn), FastAPI, PostgreSQL with pgvector, fastembed (bge-small-en-v1.5 embeddings), open-weight language models served by Groq (Qwen / gpt-oss), plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript with SVG charts; deployed on Railway and Cloudflare Pages. BASS (PSI-26): solid materials, shown as evidence
